item.title: US adds just 29,000 jobs as unemployment rises before midterm elections
item.description:
The US labor market added 29,000 jobs in September, falling far short of economists’ expectations following a strong showing in August, and the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%. Downward revisions for July and August also point to a weaker labor market than first though. The report adds to evidence that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady at its October meeting. Traders in fed funds futures curtailed bets on a Fed rate hike , per CME Fedwatch, and the 10-year Treasury yield slid about 6 basis points after nearing its highest level since 2002. But fresh inflation data expected next week will factor into the central bank’s decision. “Continued pressure by markets and moves higher in energy prices could force the Fed’s hand this month ,” a bond investor told CNBC. — Jake Angelo

item.title: What we know about Tennessee's botched execution of Christa Pike
item.description:
On Wednesday night, the state of Tennessee failed to execute Christa Pike, a convicted murderer , despite giving her a double dose of a drug that was meant to kill her. Since then, Pike has been in critical condition and is receiving medical attention, according to her lawyers, and has reignited a fierce debate about the role of the death penalty in the criminal justice system. Among those rattled by the incident is Frank Thompson, the former superintendent of the Oregon State Penitentiary. The state has carried out only two executions over the past 60 years, in 1996 and 1997. Thompson planned and oversaw both of them, including construction of the room where the two men died by lethal injection . item.description:
On Sept. 16, a student at Cornell University filed a lawsuit against the university, fraternities, and sororities after she was allegedly drugged and gang-raped by seven fraternity brothers in 2024. The allegations are horrifying. But just as troubling is what the lawsuit describes afterward: a survivor seeking help from the systems meant to protect her and finding, again and again, that she was failed. In 2026, we are still asking how this happened. The Cornell case is not only about the conduct alleged in one lawsuit. It is about a broader failure of prevention, investigation, and accountability —one that survivors of sexual violence encounter far too often, on campuses and far beyond them.
